POLICY BRIEF TO THE
PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
Protecting Private Property Rights and Reforming
Transmission-Line Need, Routing, Notice, and Procurement Procedures
Using PUC Docket No. 59475 — Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation
765-kV Transmission Line Project — as a Case Study
Submitted by
Aaron “Eddy” Howton
Salado, Texas
August 12, 2026

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Texas must expand and reinforce its electric transmission system when reliability and public necessity require it. But the State should not treat privately owned farms, ranches, homes, churches, and family property as the default location for new transmission corridors merely because condemnation is legally available. Private property is not an unlimited planning resource. It is a constitutionally protected interest, often representing generations of work, family history, agricultural investment, and community identity.
This brief asks the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission or PUC) to reform its certificate of convenience and necessity (CCN) policies so that avoidance of unnecessary burdens on private property becomes a first-priority routing principle. The existing rules already direct utilities to moderate impacts on affected communities and landowners, consider existing compatible rights-of-way, roads, highways, railroads, property lines, and prudent avoidance. The next step should be to make those principles operational, measurable, and enforceable before greenfield private property is selected.
The Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV project in PUC Docket No. 59475 illustrates why reform is needed. The project is unprecedented in scale for many affected communities. Public participation meetings occurred in June 2025, yet route concepts changed afterward. When the application was filed on March 26, 2026, additional landowners were placed within the formally proposed routing network and received formal CCN notice only after filing. The applicants maintain that their formal notice complied with the existing rule, and the administrative law judges found notice legally sufficient. Nevertheless, affected landowners have identified a real procedural inequity: landowners added after the earlier public meetings did not receive the same advance opportunity to study the project, attend a meeting concerning routes that actually affected them, identify errors, retain assistance, coordinate with neighbors, or influence route development before the CCN filing.
That disparity demonstrates a policy gap even if the minimum formal-notice rule was technically satisfied. A fair process should provide substantially equivalent participation opportunities to every landowner whose property may ultimately be placed on a filed route. The Commission should not allow route development to create a class of early-notified landowners with months of preparation and a second class of newly affected landowners who enter the process only when the formal litigation clock is already running.
I. PURPOSE OF THIS POLICY BRIEF
The purpose of this brief is broader than the selection of a single route in Docket No. 59475. It asks the Commission to use the lessons of that proceeding to improve Texas transmission policy prospectively. Texas will need new transmission facilities, but reliability should be achieved through a process that is transparent, independently verified, cost-disciplined, and designed from the beginning to minimize unnecessary use of private property.
The Commission’s present legal framework recognizes landowner impacts, but those impacts can become only one set of factors among many after utilities have already developed a large routing network. By that point, the central planning assumptions, study area, voltage choice, endpoints, route links, and engineering preferences may already channel the decision toward new private easements. A better policy would protect property rights upstream—during need determination, corridor planning, alternatives analysis, and public notice—not merely after a landowner has been placed on a proposed route.
II. PRIVATE PROPERTY RIGHTS SHOULD BE A FIRST-PRIORITY ROUTING PRINCIPLE
Article I, section 17 of the Texas Constitution protects private property from being taken, damaged, or destroyed for public use without adequate compensation. Compensation is essential, but compensation alone does not answer the routing question. The policy question before the Commission is whether a particular family, farm, ranch, church, or business should be subjected to a new transmission corridor at all when a reasonably feasible, less-injurious alternative exists.
PURA §37.056 requires the Commission to consider need, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and other public-interest factors. In addition, 16 Texas Administrative Code §25.101(b)(3)(B) states that, considering the statutory criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, a transmission line must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. The rule further requires consideration of existing compatible electric rights-of-way, roads, highways, railroads and other compatible rights-of-way, property lines and natural or cultural features, and prudent avoidance.
These existing principles should be strengthened into a clear hierarchy. The Commission should adopt a policy that new private-property acquisition is a last-resort routing tool rather than the first practical option. The existence of eminent-domain authority should never be treated as a substitute for proving that less-injurious alternatives were meaningfully investigated.
Recommended routing hierarchy
First, maximize use of existing transmission corridors and vacant positions on existing compatible facilities where technically feasible.
Second, evaluate compatible public transportation, utility, railroad, and other established rights-of-way.
Third, evaluate available governmental or public land, including federal property where an easement or right-of-way mechanism may lawfully be available and compatible with the governmental mission.
Fourth, when new private property cannot reasonably be avoided, follow property boundaries and other features that reduce fragmentation and minimize effects on homes, agricultural operations, cultural resources, and community institutions.
Fifth, require the applicant to explain on the record why each less-injurious category was rejected before approving a route that creates substantial new private easements.
This would not create an absolute prohibition on private-property crossings. Grid reliability, safety, engineering feasibility, environmental law, military operations, cost, and other constraints may make a private route necessary. But the burden should be on the applicant to demonstrate necessity and comparative reasonableness, not on individual landowners to prove after the fact that some other corridor should have been investigated.
III. INDEPENDENT DETERMINATION OF NEED, SCALE, AND ALTERNATIVES
A 765-kV transmission system of this magnitude warrants an unusually high level of independence and transparency. The concern is not whether Oncor or LCRA TSC are technically capable of building transmission facilities. The concern is institutional: an entity that will own regulated assets and recover approved costs has a financial interest in project scale and capital investment. That does not establish misconduct, but it is a sufficient reason for independent verification before thousands of acres of private property are subjected to new easements.
Before landowners face condemnation, permanent corridors, or restrictions on the future use of their property, Texas should require a verified determination of the actual capacity required, the timing and location of that need, and the reasonableness of the assumptions used to forecast load growth. The Commission and ERCOT should not rely exclusively on utility-developed projections when the consequence of those projections is a very large capital program paid by ratepayers and borne physically by landowners.
At a minimum, independent review should address:
Actual and reasonably foreseeable load growth supported by verifiable evidence;
The credibility and probability of projected large-load additions, including the maturity of the underlying projects;
The true incremental capacity need rather than simply the amount of capacity a proposed system could accommodate;
Alternatives such as 345-kV upgrades, use of existing corridors, generation, storage, demand-side resources, or different staging and timing;
Comparative reliability and resiliency benefits of a 765-kV solution;
Full ratepayer effects, including capital, financing, operating, and long-term revenue requirements; and
Landowner, agricultural, community, environmental, historical, cultural, and aesthetic consequences of the project configuration.
The independent need and alternatives analysis should be completed before the routing process has advanced so far that the basic project configuration becomes practically irreversible.
IV. INDEPENDENT ENGINEERING AND COMPETITIVE PROCUREMENT
If the Commission determines that a major project is necessary, the engineering requirements should be independently validated before the final design is effectively locked in. To the extent permitted by Texas law and the structure of the transmission market, construction or major project components should then be competitively procured among qualified entities based on price, technical capability, reliability, schedule, and accountability.
The objective is not to exclude Oncor, LCRA TSC, or any other experienced transmission provider. It is to separate the public-interest questions: (1) whether capacity is needed, (2) what technical solution best meets the need, (3) what corridor approach least injures landowners and communities while satisfying reliability, and (4) which entity can construct the approved facilities efficiently. Separation of these decisions improves transparency and helps protect both ratepayers and landowners.
V. PUBLIC AND EXISTING RIGHTS-OF-WAY MUST BE ACTUALLY INVESTIGATED, NOT ASSUMED AWAY
The source material for this brief identifies a significant routing-policy issue: before substantial new private-property easements are authorized, the record should show whether existing public, federal, military, transportation, and utility corridors were actually investigated and, if rejected, why. A general statement that a governmental easement may be difficult, costly, or subject to agency approval is not equivalent to an actual feasibility inquiry.
For example, the Bell County East–Big Hill study area includes federal property and major governmental holdings, including the Fort Hood area and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers property associated with Stillhouse Hollow Lake. The relevant policy question is not whether every acre of federal land is available. Much of it may be unavailable for legitimate military, environmental, operational, security, or statutory reasons. The required question should be whether an applicant identified potential corridors, contacted the controlling agency, investigated available right-of-way authority, evaluated engineering feasibility, and documented any agency rejection or other constraint before turning to new private easements.
The same principle applies to existing highways, railroads, transmission corridors, pipelines, and other compatible rights-of-way. The Commission should require a route-by-route accounting of how much new private right-of-way is created and what existing corridor opportunities were evaluated. A route that is slightly shorter or cheaper should not automatically prevail if it imposes substantially greater new private-property burdens that could reasonably be avoided.
VI. DOCKET NO. 59475 DEMONSTRATES A SERIOUS NOTICE AND PARTICIPATION PROBLEM
The Bell County East–Big Hill proceeding provides a concrete example of why the notice rules should be revised. Oncor and LCRA TSC held three public participation meetings on June 16–18, 2025. Their own current project information acknowledges that the public-meeting materials reflected the information available at that time and that the filed application was later updated. The CCN application was filed on March 26, 2026, with an intervention deadline of April 27, 2026.
Affected landowners have asserted that the preliminary routing network expanded or materially changed after the June 2025 meetings, resulting in a substantial group of landowners first learning that their property could be affected only after the March 2026 filing. Public reporting described approximately 2,800 landowners associated with the earlier public-meeting notice and approximately 4,200 landowners receiving notice after the CCN filing. Oncor disputes that this constituted a notice violation and has stated that all formal notice required by 16 Texas Administrative Code §22.52 was provided after filing, including notice to owners within approximately 520 feet of the proposed routes. The administrative law judges found the formal notice legally sufficient.
The Commission should not allow that legal finding to end the policy inquiry. The issue raised by Docket No. 59475 is whether the rule itself assures equal and meaningful participation when route links are added or changed after public meetings. It currently permits a situation in which one group of landowners may know for many months that a project could affect them and can attend a public meeting, submit route information, identify resources, organize, retain counsel, and influence route development, while another group enters the process only after the final routing network is filed and the intervention and litigation schedule begins.
That is not equivalent participation. For property owners facing potential condemnation, a procedural difference of many months is substantive. The value of public participation lies not only in receiving a letter; it lies in having a fair opportunity to influence routing before the applicant’s choices harden into a filed CCN case.
VII. PROPOSED NOTICE AND PROCEDURAL REFORMS
The Commission should amend its rules or adopt formal policy guidance to prevent the notice disparity illustrated by Docket No. 59475.
Supplemental pre-filing notice for new routes. If an applicant adds or materially relocates a route link after a public participation meeting and the change creates newly affected landowners, those landowners should receive direct notice before the CCN filing.
Supplemental public meeting requirement. If a material post-meeting route change creates a meaningful number of newly affected landowners, the applicant should conduct a supplemental public participation meeting in the affected area before filing.
Comparable participation period. Newly affected landowners should receive a reasonable period to investigate the project and submit routing information before the applicant finalizes its CCN application. The Commission should establish a minimum period rather than allowing the amount of preparation time to depend on when a route link was added.
Deadline protection after late or supplemental notice. When an owner is added late, intervention, testimony, discovery, and other material participation deadlines should be extended as necessary to provide a meaningful opportunity to participate, consistent with the policy reflected in §22.52(a)(5) and the late-intervention protections in the procedural rules.
Disclosure of route-change history. Every CCN filing should include a route-change log showing when each link was created, modified, or removed, why the change was made, what landowners became newly affected, and when those landowners were notified.
No preferential route development through unequal access. Applicants should disclose substantive pre-filing contacts concerning route movement or creation and should certify that route changes were evaluated under objective criteria rather than on the comparative ability of particular landowners to retain counsel, lobby the utility, or participate early.
Field verification before filing. Applicants should verify critical habitable-structure, community, historical, cultural, agricultural, and environmental information sufficiently to prevent desktop or aerial-data errors from shifting burdens onto landowners who have little time to correct the record.
VIII. REQUIRE A PRIVATE-PROPERTY IMPACT SCORE FOR EVERY ALTERNATIVE ROUTE
The Commission already evaluates numerous route characteristics. A specific private-property impact score would make the landowner burden visible rather than implicit. Each alternative route should disclose, in a standardized format:
Total acres of new private easement required;
Miles of new greenfield private right-of-way versus miles using or paralleling existing compatible corridors;
Number of separate private owners crossed;
Number and type of habitable structures within the applicable distance;
Number of farms, ranches, homesteads, churches, schools, cemeteries, businesses, and other community institutions directly affected;
Degree of property fragmentation and interference with existing agricultural, ranching, wildlife-management, or commercial use;
Known historical, archaeological, cultural, aesthetic, and environmental resources;
Existing public or governmental corridor alternatives investigated and the specific basis for rejection; and
Estimated acquisition cost together with non-monetary landowner and community impacts.
The Commission should require an express finding when it selects a route with materially greater new private-property burden than another reasonably feasible alternative. The finding should explain what reliability, engineering, environmental, or public-interest consideration justified the additional burden.
IX. ROUTING SHOULD NOT BE DRIVEN BY COST ALONE
Cost matters because ratepayers ultimately pay for regulated transmission investment. But the lowest apparent construction or easement cost is not necessarily the least-cost public solution when it externalizes major consequences onto private owners. A complete comparison should account for property fragmentation, impacts on future use, agricultural operations, community institutions, cultural and historical resources, litigation risk, environmental mitigation, and the long-term value of preserving established corridors rather than creating new ones.
The Commission should therefore reject any policy—explicit or implicit—that allows a modest savings in route length or initial acquisition cost to outweigh a substantially greater and avoidable private-property impact without a written public-interest justification.
X. SPECIFIC POLICY ACTIONS REQUESTED OF THE COMMISSION
1.  Initiate a rulemaking or policy project to make minimization of new private-property burdens a first-priority routing principle, subject to reliability, safety, engineering feasibility, environmental law, and reasonable cost constraints.
2.  Amend 16 Texas Administrative Code §25.101 or associated CCN forms to require a standardized Private Property Impact Analysis for every proposed route.
3.  Amend 16 Texas Administrative Code §22.52 to require supplemental direct notice and, when warranted, a supplemental public meeting for material post-meeting route changes that create newly affected landowners.
4.  Establish minimum comparable preparation rights for landowners who are first affected by late route additions, including extensions of intervention and procedural deadlines when necessary for meaningful participation.
5.  Require applicants to document investigation of existing transmission corridors, highways, railroads, utility corridors, public lands, federal lands, and other compatible rights-of-way before approving routes that require substantial new greenfield private easements.
6.  Require independent review of need, scale, voltage, and major alternatives for projects of extraordinary size or cost before final route development.
7.  Require applicants to provide a route-change history identifying when and why route links were added, altered, or removed and when newly affected owners were notified.
8.  Require sufficient field verification of route data before filing so that affected landowners are not forced to correct material omissions under compressed litigation deadlines.
9.  Require an express Commission finding whenever the approved route places materially greater burdens on private property than a reasonably feasible alternative, explaining why that burden is necessary in the public interest.
10.  Evaluate whether competitive procurement or other independent construction-selection mechanisms can be expanded for major transmission projects after need, specifications, and routing requirements have been independently established.
XI. CONCLUSION
Reliable electricity is essential to Texas, but reliability and private-property rights are not opposing values. A disciplined transmission policy can protect both. The Commission’s responsibility is not merely to determine whether a transmission line can be built; it is to determine whether the proposed project and route are necessary, reasonable, and in the public interest after the burdens have been fairly compared.
Docket No. 59475 shows why the process should change. The project illustrates the consequences of designing an enormous routing network first and then requiring individual landowners to defend their property under a compressed procedural schedule. It also illustrates a notice structure that can provide early participation to one group of landowners while leaving later-added landowners with only the formal post-filing process. Even where an applicant satisfies the minimum notice rule, the State should demand a process that is equally fair in substance.
Texas policy should begin with a simple principle: private property should not be taken or burdened for a transmission corridor unless the need is independently established and the applicant has demonstrated that reasonably feasible, less-injurious alternatives have been seriously investigated. Existing corridors and public or governmental rights-of-way should be examined first; new private greenfield easements should be used only when necessary and justified on the record.
The Commission has the opportunity to strengthen public confidence in future transmission development by making property protection, equal notice, independent verification, transparent route comparison, and accountable procurement central features of the CCN process. Those reforms would not prevent Texas from building the transmission system it needs. They would ensure that Texas builds it in a manner worthy of the property rights, communities, and ratepayers the system is intended to serve.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Aaron E. Howton
Aaron “Eddy” Howton
Salado, Texas
August 12, 2026

approximately 4,200 landowners receiving notice after the CCN filing. Oncor disputes that this
constituted a notice violation and has stated that all formal notice required by 16 Texas
Administrative Code §22.52 was provided after filing, including notice to owners within
approximately 520 feet of the proposed routes. The administrative law judges found the formal
notice legally sufficient.
     The Commission should not allow that legal finding to end the policy inquiry. The issue raised
by Docket No. 59475 is whether the rule itself assures equal and meaningful participation when
route links are added or changed after public meetings. It currently permits a situation in which
one group of landowners may know for many months that a project could affect them and can
attend a public meeting, submit route information, identify resources, organize, retain counsel, and
influence route development, while another group enters the process only after the final routing
network is filed and the intervention and litigation schedule begins.
    That is not equivalent participation. For property owners facing potential condemnation, a
procedural difference of many months is substantive. The value of public participation lies not
only in receiving a letter; it lies in having a fair opportunity to influence routing before the
applicant' s choices harden into a filed CCN case.

VII. PROPOSED NOTICE AND PROCEDURAL REFORMS
    The Commission should amend its rules or adopt formal policy guidance to prevent the notice
disparity illustrated by Docket No. 59475.
Supplemental pre-filing notice for new routes. If an applicant adds or materially relocates a
  route link after a public participation meeting and the change creates newly affected
  landowners, those landowners should receive direct notice before the CCN filing.
Supplemental public meeting requirement. If a material post-meeting route change creates a
  meaningful number of newly affected landowners, the applicant should conduct a
  supplemental public participation meeting in the affected area before filing.


                                                Page 6
 Comparable participation period. Newly affected landowners should receive a reasonable
  period to investigate the project and submit routing information before the applicant finalizes
  its CCN application. The Commission should establish a minimum period rather than
  allowing the amount of preparation time to depend on when a route link was added.
Deadline protection after late or supplemental notice. When an owner is added late,
    intervention, testimony, discovery, and other material participation deadlines should be
    extended as necessary to provide a meaningful opportunity to participate, consistent with the
    policy reflected in §22.52(a)(5) and the late-intervention protections in the procedural rules.
Disclosure of route-change history. Every CCN filing should include a route-change log
   showing when each link was created, modified, or removed, why the change was made, what
   landowners became newly affected, and when those landowners were notified.
No preferential route development through unequal access. Applicants should disclose
  substantive pre-filing contacts concerning route movement or creation and should certify that
  route changes were evaluated under objective criteria rather than on the comparative ability of
  particular landowners to retain counsel, lobby the utility, or participate early.
Field verification before filing. Applicants should verify critical habitable-structure,
    community, historical, cultural, agricultural, and environmental information sufficiently to
    prevent desktop or aerial-data errors from shifting burdens onto landowners who have little
    time to correct the record.

VIII. REQUIRE A PRIVATE-PROPERTY IMPACT SCORE FOR EVERY
ALTERNATIVE ROUTE
    The Commission already evaluates numerous route characteristics. A specific private-
property impact score would make the landowner burden visible rather than implicit. Each
alternative route should disclose, in a standardized format:
•   Total acres of new private easement required;
•   Miles of new greenfield private right-of-way versus miles using or paralleling existing
    compatible corridors;
•   Number of separate private owners crossed;
•   Number and type of habitable structures within the applicable distance;
•   Number of farms, ranches, homesteads, churches, schools, cemeteries, businesses, and other
    community institutions directly affected;
•   Degree of property fragmentation and interference with existing agricultural, ranching,
    wildlife-management, or commercial use;
•   Known historical, archaeological, cultural, aesthetic, and environmental resources;
•   Existing public or governmental corridor alternatives investigated and the specific basis for
    rejection; and
•   Estimated acquisition cost together with non-monetary landowner and community impacts.
    The Commission should require an express finding when it selects a route with materially
greater new private-property burden than another reasonably feasible alternative. The finding



                                                Page 7
  should explain what reliability, engineering, environmental, or public-interest consideration
justified the additional burden.

IX. ROUTING SHOULD NOT BE DRIVEN BY COST ALONE
     Cost matters because ratepayers ultimately pay for regulated transmission investment. But the
lowest apparent construction or easement cost is not necessarily the least-cost public solution when
it externalizes major consequences onto private owners. A complete comparison should account
for property fragmentation, impacts on future use, agricultural operations, community institutions,
cultural and historical resources, litigation risk, environmental mitigation, and the long-term value
of preserving established corridors rather than creating new ones.
    The Commission should therefore reject any policy-explicit or implicit -that allows a
modest savings in route length or initial acquisition cost to outweigh a substantially greater and
avoidable private-property impact without a written public-interest justification.

X. SPECIFIC POLICY ACTIONS REQUESTED OF THE COMMISSION
1. Initiate a rulemaking or policy project to make minimization of new private-property burdens
     a first-priority routing principle, subject to reliability, safety, engineering feasibility,
     environmental law, and reasonable cost constraints.
2. Amend 16 Texas Administrative Code §25.101 or associated CCN forms to require a
    standardized Private Property Impact Analysis for every proposed route.
3. Amend 16 Texas Administrative Code §22.52 to require supplemental direct notice and, when
    warranted, a supplemental public meeting for material post-meeting route changes that
    create newly affected landowners.
4. Establish minimum comparable preparation rights for landowners who are first affected by
    late route additions, including extensions of intervention and procedural deadlines when
    necessary for meaningful participation.
5. Require applicants to document investigation of existing transmission corridors, highways,
    railroads, utility corridors, public lands, federal lands, and other compatible rights-of-way
    before approving routes that require substantial new greenfield private easements.
6. Require independent review of need, scale, voltage, and major alternatives for projects of
     extraordinary size or cost before final route development.
7. Require applicants to provide a route-change history identifying when and why route links
    were added, altered, or removed and when newly affected owners were notified.
8. Require sufficient field verification of route data before filing so that affected landowners are
    not forced to correct material omissions under compressed litigation deadlines.
9. Require an express Commission finding whenever the approved route places materially
    greater burdens on private property than a reasonably feasible alternative, explaining why
    that burden is necessary in the public interest.
10. Evaluate whether competitive procurement or other independent construction-selection
    mechanisms can be expanded for major transmission projects after need, specifications, and
    routing requirements have been independently established.

 XI. CONCLUSION
    Reliable electricity is essential to Texas, but reliability and private-property rights are not
opposing values. A disciplined transmission policy can protect both. The Commission' s
responsibility is not merely to determine whether a transmission line can be built; it is to determine
whether the proposed project and route are necessary, reasonable, and in the public interest after
the burdens have been fairly compared.
     Docket No. 59475 shows why the process should change. The project illustrates the
consequences of designing an enormous routing network first and then requiring individual
landowners to defend their property under a compressed procedural schedule. It also illustrates a
notice structure that can provide early participation to one group of landowners while leaving later-
added landowners with only the formal post-filing process. Even where an applicant satisfies the
minimum notice rule, the State should demand a process that is equally fair in substance.
     Texas policy should begin with a simple principle: private property should not be taken or
burdened for a transmission corridor unless the need is independently established and the applicant
has demonstrated that reasonably feasible, less-injurious alternatives have been seriously
investigated. Existing corridors and public or governmental rights-of-way should be examined
first; new private greenfield easements should be used only when necessary and justified on the
record.
     The Commission has the opportunity to strengthen public confidence in future transmission
development by making property protection, equal notice, independent verification, transparent
route comparison, and accountable procurement central features of the CCN process. Those
reforms would not prevent Texas from building the transmission system it needs. They would
ensure that Texas builds it in a manner worthy ofthe property rights, communities, and ratepayers
the system is intended to serve.
